programs.name: North Dakota Basic Care Assistance Program (BCAP)
programs.tagline: Helps cover the cost of basic care facility services for eligible North Dakota seniors and disabled adults.
programs.intro:
If your loved one needs help with daily activities like bathing, dressing, or eating and lives in a licensed basic care facility, North Dakota's Basic Care Assistance Program (BCAP) may help cover facility costs. BCAP pays a portion of basic care facility expenses for people who qualify for North Dakota Medicaid and need assistance with activities of daily living. Your loved one keeps $150 per month for personal needs, while their other income goes toward facility costs and BCAP covers the remaining expenses directly to the facility.

To qualify, your loved one must be 65+ (or 18+ if blind or disabled), meet North Dakota Medicaid income and asset requirements (typically $3,000 asset limit for singles), and pass a functional assessment showing they need help with daily activities. Because this program requires living in a licensed basic care facility, it's designed for people who cannot safely remain at home even with assistance.

BCAP is administered through the same system as Medicaid, so if your loved one already receives Medicaid long-term care services, the eligibility process may be streamlined through redetermination rather than a completely new application.
programs.savingsSource: Varies by income - program covers facility costs beyond what recipient can pay

steps.title: Check Medicaid eligibility first
steps.description: Since BCAP requires North Dakota Medicaid qualification, ensure your loved one meets Medicaid income and asset requirements. If already on Medicaid, this may be handled through redetermination.

steps.title: Submit application
steps.description: Apply online through the Customer Support Center's Apply for Assistance portal, call (866) 614-6005, or email applyforhelp@nd.gov. You can also mail forms to Customer Support Center, P.O. Box 5562, Bismarck, ND 58506.

steps.description: A county social worker will conduct a Personal Care Services Assessment to determine if your loved one needs help with activities of daily living like bathing, dressing, or eating.

steps.description: Your loved one must reside in a licensed basic care facility in North Dakota. Contact agingbcreferrals@nd.gov for assistance with facility referrals.

faqs.question: Can my loved one apply for BCAP if they're already receiving North Dakota Medicaid?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your loved one already receives North Dakota Medicaid, BCAP eligibility may be processed through redetermination rather than requiring a completely new application. Contact the Customer Support Center at (866) 614-6005 to discuss the specific process for current Medicaid recipients.

faqs.question: What's the difference between basic care facilities and nursing homes for BCAP eligibility?
faqs.answer: BCAP specifically covers costs for licensed basic care facilities, not nursing homes. Basic care facilities provide assistance with activities of daily living but offer less intensive medical care than nursing facilities. Some applicants may need to have resided in a nursing facility for at least 6 months before qualifying for BCAP in certain circumstances.

faqs.question: How much of my loved one's income will go toward facility costs?
faqs.answer: Your loved one keeps $150 per month for personal needs. All other income must be applied toward facility costs and medical expenses, with BCAP covering the remaining facility expenses directly. The exact amount BCAP pays depends on your loved one's total income and the facility's costs.

faqs.question: What if my loved one needs nursing home level care but wants to try basic care first?
faqs.answer: This requires careful coordination with healthcare providers and the county social worker doing the functional assessment. The assessment must show that basic care facility services are appropriate for your loved one's needs. Contact agingbcreferrals@nd.gov to discuss facility options and care level requirements.

faqs.question: Can I apply for BCAP on behalf of my elderly loved one?
faqs.answer: Yes, family members can typically apply on behalf of elderly loved ones, especially if the loved one has cognitive impairment or difficulty managing paperwork. You may need to provide documentation of your authority to act on their behalf, such as power of attorney documents.

faqs.question: What happens if my loved one's care needs increase while on BCAP?
faqs.answer: If your loved one's care needs change significantly, they'll need a new functional assessment. This could result in a recommendation for a different level of care, such as nursing facility placement, which would involve transitioning to different Medicaid long-term care services.

faqs.question: Are there any assets my loved one can keep while on BCAP?
faqs.answer: BCAP follows North Dakota Medicaid asset rules, which typically allow $3,000 in countable assets for single individuals. However, specific exemptions and rules for what counts as assets aren't detailed in BCAP program materials - contact the Customer Support Center at (866) 614-6005 for specific guidance about your loved one's assets.

faqs.question: What if there are no licensed basic care facilities available in my loved one's area?
faqs.answer: Contact agingbcreferrals@nd.gov for assistance finding available licensed basic care facilities statewide. While your loved one must be a North Dakota resident, they don't necessarily need to stay in their current community if appropriate facilities aren't available locally.

programs.name: North Dakota Aging in Community (AIC) Project
programs.tagline: Community volunteers help your loved one stay safely at home in rural North Dakota, transportation, fall prevention, and local connections.

localEntities.name: NDSU Extension Service (Lisbon, western Morton Counties)

programs.intro:
If your loved one lives in rural North Dakota and wants to stay at home but needs help with transportation, learning about technology, or connecting with local resources, the Aging in Community Project may provide volunteer assistance at no cost. Because this is a community-based pilot program, it's only available in select rural areas like Lisbon and western Morton Counties.

The program focuses on practical daily support, volunteer drivers for medical appointments, nutrition and fall prevention classes, help learning to use smartphones or tablets, and connections to other local services. Because it relies on volunteers and local partnerships rather than paid staff, the specific services vary by location but all aim to help older adults remain safely independent in their rural homes.

summary: Desire to age in place at home
otherRequirements: Living in implementation areas such as Lisbon and western Morton Counties

faqs.question: Is this program available where my loved one lives?
faqs.answer: The AIC Project operates only in select rural communities like Lisbon and western Morton Counties. Contact your local NDSU Extension office to confirm if your loved one's area is served, as this is a pilot program with limited geographic reach.

faqs.question: What if my loved one needs more intensive help than volunteers can provide?
faqs.answer: The AIC Project focuses on community connections and prevention rather than medical care or intensive daily assistance. If your loved one needs help with bathing, medication management, or clinical care, ask the coordinator about referrals to programs like SPED or Medicaid waiver services.

faqs.question: Can my loved one count on regular transportation every week?
faqs.answer: Transportation depends on volunteer driver availability in your specific community, so it may not be as reliable as paid services. Ask the local coordinator about typical availability and consider this as supplemental to other transportation arrangements.

faqs.question: How is this different from other aging services in North Dakota?
faqs.answer: Unlike SPED (which pays for services) or Medicaid waivers (which provide clinical care), the AIC Project uses volunteers to build community connections and teach practical skills. It's designed to prevent isolation and help people stay independent longer, not replace medical services.

faqs.question: What happens if my loved one moves to a different rural town?
faqs.answer: If your loved one moves outside an active AIC project area, they would no longer be eligible for services. The program is location-specific and depends on local volunteer networks and NDSU Extension partnerships in each community.

programs.name: ND Assistive Senior Safety Program
programs.tagline: Free safety devices shipped to your loved one at home, to help them stay there safely

localEntities.name: Central office: 3240 15th St. S, Suite B, Fargo, ND 58104

programs.intro:
If your loved one is 60 or older and needs safety devices to remain at home, ND Assistive can send equipment at no cost. The program covers alerting devices for hearing loss, anti-elopement devices for dementia care, and other home safety equipment. Devices are shipped to the home. If they also want help choosing or setting equipment up, ND Assistive offers a separate home safety evaluation you can ask about on the same call.

There is no income limit and you do not need to be turned down by insurance, Medicare, or Medicaid first. Funding is limited and this is not an entitlement, so requests are prioritized: preference goes to people living outside Bismarck, Grand Forks, and Fargo, people at risk of moving into a nursing facility, and households with income below the federal poverty level. You will rank the devices you need in order of importance on the application.
programs.savingsSource: Free service. Funding is limited and this is not an entitlement program.

faqs.question: What if my loved one lives in assisted living, can they still get these devices?
faqs.answer: Yes, the program is available to seniors in assisted living facilities if they need additional safety devices beyond what the facility provides. The application process is the same.

faqs.question: Does my loved one have to be turned down by Medicare or Medicaid first?
faqs.answer: No. There is no requirement to be denied by insurance, Medicare, or Medicaid before applying. The application does ask whether they are enrolled in Medicare, Medicaid, or Northland PACE, but that is so ND Assistive can coordinate, not a hurdle. Apply directly.

faqs.question: How many devices can my loved one receive through this program?
faqs.answer: The application doesn't specify a limit, but you must rank devices in order of importance because the program may not approve everything you request. Priority is given based on safety need and available funding.

programs.name: North Dakota Family Caregiver Support Program
programs.tagline: Help for unpaid caregivers, including a caregiver coordinator, counseling, training, respite breaks and some supplies.
programs.intro:
North Dakota Family Caregiver Support Program helps unpaid family caregivers keep going. Help for unpaid caregivers, including a caregiver coordinator, counseling, training, respite breaks and some supplies.

Help can include information about local services, a trained caregiver coordinator, counseling, support groups and training, respite care for caregivers who provide 24-hour care and supplemental services such as incontinence supplies and shower benches.

Call the ND Aging and Disability Resource-LINK (TTY 711), email carechoice@nd.gov, or apply online at ND Care Choice. Services are free to qualifying people; caregivers may choose to contribute.

stateOverview.intro: North Dakota offers 3 key programs to help your aging loved one stay safe and supported. Two provide direct financial assistance for care services, while one offers free safety resources for any North Dakota senior. The Basic Care Assistance Program helps cover facility care costs, the Aging in Community Project provides volunteer support specifically in rural areas, and the Assistive Senior Safety Program delivers free safety devices with professional installation. Start by identifying your loved one's most immediate need, whether that's paying for care, staying connected in a rural community, or making their home safer.

stateOverview.resourcesVsBenefits: North Dakota offers both types of help: qualification-based benefits like BCAP that require income and asset screening to help pay for care, and free resources like the Assistive Senior Safety Program that any North Dakota senior can access regardless of income. The AIC Project falls in between, it's free but specifically serves rural communities where volunteer networks are available.
